reasons.agent: The follow-up task changes the build's state rules and can spend quota unattended, which is the Opus case.
reasons.builder: Opus for the follow-up task; Sonnet for the drive, record and recommendation tasks, which are routine, to save quota.
reasons.checker: QA tests by running the product and builds none of this.
reasons.mode: Four tasks in order, each depending on the last; a flow runs them without hand-offs.
reasons.stop: Stop when the four tasks are done.

design:
**Slice boundary.** The Build dialog only gains a reason line beside each task's row; its redesign is the next slice. No new person fields: this uses the task `builder` and `checker` the build-plan slice shipped.

**The author judges, and the operator chooses its sources (operator, 2026-11-01).** Before naming people, the author says what it currently believes about the roster's models and asks which of three sources to use, any combination: agree with what it already knows, search the web for current prices and models, or review how the models performed in this project. A web search or review costs a turn's quota, which is why it is the operator's call. A `fix`-size document skips the question and uses what the author knows, because the prompt would outweigh the work.

**This widens a roadmap non-goal, by the operator's decision.** The roadmap excluded inputs other than model, cost and complexity, naming "who built similar work before". Performance is now an input, measured per model and never per agent: an agent's model can change, and ranking named agents is still out.

**What the project review reads.** Per model: tasks built, how often each was sent back and for which `reason_class`, and API-equivalent cost. These are counts, not a verdict: a model given only hard tasks is sent back more, so the author states the sample size and weighs the figures itself.

```
TODAY     last task approved -> build finished -> flow ended
          follow-up filed    -> no build, no people, nobody starts it
PROPOSED  follow-up filed    -> build reopens -> its people -> a new flow starts it
                             -> the Overview warns the operator, who can stop it
```

**Always reopen, and warn (operator, 2026-11-01).** A finished build reopens however long ago it finished. The operator chose this over a time limit: nothing is stranded, and managing an unwanted restart is theirs, so the warning is what makes the rule safe. It sits on the Overview screen (operator, 2026-11-01), and it fires on every reopening, because a restart nobody asked for is exactly the case it exists for.

**Reopening starts a new flow, not an old one.** A finished flow is ended and is not resumed. The build gets a fresh flow from its recorded settings, as `_joined_build` already does (`api/v1/spec.py:3637`), and the work branches from current main.

**A stop is a decision; a finish is not.** A build the operator stopped, or one stopped by its budget cap or window, stays stopped.

open_questions.question: Who makes the recommendation? Answer: the author agent (operator, 2026-11-01).
How is cost and performance judged? Answer: from what the author knows, after asking the operator whether to agree with that, search the web, or review this project's work (operator, 2026-11-01).
How long after a build finishes can a follow-up reopen it? Answer: always, with a warning in the Hub so the operator can manage it (operator, 2026-11-01).
Where does the reopening warning appear? Answer: the Overview screen (operator, 2026-11-01).

problem:
Nothing asks an author to choose people per task. The writing steps say to name a task's own `builder` or `checker` only where it differs from the delivery's (`spec_journey.py:537`), so most tasks arrive at Build on the defaults and the operator works out the split by hand. A task can name people, and Build pre-fills them (`BuildDialog.tsx:78-87`), but nowhere holds a reason per pick: `Delivery.reasons` covers build-wide choices only (`spec_payload.py:325`). The Build step's text also still asks for reasons keyed `reviewer` and `tester` (`spec_journey.py:550-551`), names the slice before it replaced with `checker`.

An author's sense of which model suits what comes from general knowledge, which may be out of date and says nothing about how models have done on this project. The Hub records what each turn's model cost (`TurnUsage`) and why work was sent back (`reason_class`, migration 0157), but no agent tool reads them by model, and the Hub holds no price table (`model_catalog.py`).

Follow-ups have a narrower gap than the roadmap assumed. A task filed against a document whose build is running already joins it and takes its default builder (`builds.py:560`, `api/v1/tasks.py:971`). But a build finishes the moment its last task is approved (`builds.py:781-811`), and `running_build` only finds running builds (`builds.py:96`). So a reviewer's follow-up filed after that joins nothing: it has no builder, no checker and no flow, and sits on the board until someone notices.

requirements.rationale: Naming people only where they differ from the default is why the split reaches the operator undone.
requirements.statement: An author writing a change document is asked to name a builder and a checker on every task, chosen from the open agents, each with a one-sentence reason.

The author is told each open agent's model, and each reason states the pick in terms of that model's cost and performance and the task's complexity, and nothing else. Within one document, a hazardous task and a routine task can receive different agents.

requirements.rationale: A search or review costs quota, and the operator knows whether the author's view is current.
requirements.statement: Before naming people on a document larger than a fix, the author states its current view of the roster's models and asks the operator which sources to use, in any combination: what it already knows, a web search, or a review of this project's record. It uses only those chosen, and records what it found in the document's evidence. If a chosen source is unavailable, it says so rather than presenting a guess as the finding.

requirements.rationale: The review needs figures an agent cannot otherwise reach. An agent's model can change, so attributing by agent would credit the wrong model.
requirements.statement: Any agent can read this project's record per model: tasks built, send-backs by reason class, and API-equivalent cost, each with its sample size. A task counts under the model that actually ran its build turns, and unpriced turns are reported as unpriced, not counted as zero.

requirements.rationale: A builder cannot check their own work at the Reviewed level, so such a pick could never be carried out.
requirements.statement: A task's recommended checker is never its recommended builder. When a project has one open agent, the checker is left empty and the reason says why.
Build opens with each task's recommended builder and checker selected and its reasons visible beside that task's row. The operator can change any of them, and the choice made is what is built.

requirements.rationale: Approvals are scarce: warn, do not gate (operator, 2026-10-08).
requirements.statement: A task with no recommended builder or checker, or a pick with no reason, draws a warning on the document naming the task, and never blocks approval.
When a recommended agent is no longer open at Build, the dialog says so on that task's row and does not select them. Documents with no recommendations open Build as they do today.
A task filed against a spec whose build is running goes to that build's default builder and is checked by its default checker, unless the task names its own.

A task filed against a spec whose latest build finished by running out of work reopens that build, however long ago it finished, at the same level, landing and budget cap, and takes its people as a running build's follow-up does. The build record shows that it reopened, and the spec stops reading as done until the task has landed.

requirements.rationale: The operator chose to manage unwanted restarts themselves (2026-11-01), which works only if they learn of a restart while they can still stop it.
requirements.statement: Every reopening shows the operator a warning on the Overview screen, naming the spec, the task, who filed it, and how long ago the build had finished, with a way to stop the build from the warning. The warning stays until the operator dismisses it or the build ends.

In a flow-driven build, a follow-up is started by a flow within two firings of being filed, including when the build's earlier flow had already stopped on an empty queue, with no operator or agent action. A hand-driven build's follow-up waits on the board under its builder for the operator to start.

requirements.rationale: A stop is a decision; a finish is only the absence of work. Reopening a stopped build would spend what someone chose to stop spending.
requirements.statement: A follow-up filed against a spec whose latest build was stopped, whether by the operator, its budget cap or its window, or against an archived spec, restarts nothing and shows no reopening warning. It stays on the board with no build, the filer is told why, and on a non-archived spec the operator's next Build takes it in.
Two follow-ups filed together reopen one build and one flow and show one warning naming both, and a second driver on the reopened build is refused as on any running build.

On the trial Hub, a real Haiku agent asks how to judge the models, reads the project's record when told to, and writes a spec with one hazardous and one routine task; they receive different agents with reasons and Build opens with them filled in. After that build finishes, a reviewer files a follow-up, a flow starts it under the build's people with nobody stepping in, the warning appears on the Overview screen in a browser, and stopping from it stops the build.

in_scope: The author asking the operator which sources to judge the models by
A per-model record of this project's work that agents can read
A recommended builder and checker for every task, with a reason for each
Build opening with those picks and showing their reasons
A warning, not a refusal, for a task with no recommendation or no reason
Correcting the writing steps' stale reviewer and tester wording
A follow-up filed against a spec joining its running or finished build and going to that build's people
A new flow starting a follow-up on a build whose earlier flow has ended
A warning on the Overview screen on every reopening, from which the operator can stop the build
non_goals: A time limit on reopening a finished build
Showing the reopening warning anywhere other than the Overview screen
Ranking or recommending named agents by their own past work; performance is per model
A price table or scoring rule in the Hub; the author judges
The Hub choosing the people itself
Recommendations the operator must approve as a step
An approval step before a build reopens; the operator is warned, not asked
Reopening a build the operator stopped, or one stopped by its cap or window
Starting agents automatically in a hand build
Changing what the levels Fast, Reviewed and Gated decide
Adding recommendations to documents already approved
Follow-ups on tasks with no spec

summary: While a spec is written, the author asks the operator how to judge the models (what it already knows, a web search, or a review of how they performed in this project), then gives each task a recommended builder and checker with a stated reason. Build opens with them filled in. A follow-up task filed against a spec joins its build and goes to that build's people. If the build had finished, it reopens and a new flow starts the task without anyone stepping in, and the Overview screen warns the operator, who can stop it there.
